threads_text: OpenAI plans to buy Google's AI chips, The Information reports, even though it is one of Nvidia's biggest customers. It is also hiring an engineer to tune its frontier models for Google's TPUs. Is Nvidia's lock on AI chips starting to crack?
caption:
OpenAI plans to buy Google's AI chips, called TPUs, according to The Information.
OpenAI is one of Nvidia's largest GPU buyers, and it is now hiring an engineer to tune its frontier models for TPUs.
No deal terms were reported. OpenAI declined to comment.

Is Nvidia's grip on AI chips starting to slip?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

paragraphs.text: OpenAI plans to buy artificial intelligence chips from Google, The Information reported on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, citing a person familiar with the matter. The chips in question are Google's Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, which the search company designs for training and running AI models. Reuters, which followed the report, said the financial terms and other details of the plan were not disclosed.
OpenAI declined to comment on the report, according to Reuters. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside business hours.
A major Nvidia customer looks elsewhere

OpenAI is one of the largest buyers of Nvidia's graphics processing units, which it uses both to train its models and to run them for users, a process known as inference. AI Weekly noted that Nvidia has long been OpenAI's most important chip supplier, which is why a TPU purchase stands out.

Google's TPUs have gained traction as an alternative to Nvidia hardware, Reuters reported, as companies look for cheaper options and for chips suited to running AI models. Google began selling TPUs directly to some customers in 2026. Finimize wrote that using TPUs alongside Nvidia hardware could help OpenAI diversify its supply and lower the cost of inference.

The two companies have worked together before. Reuters reported in June 2025 that OpenAI had begun renting Google's AI chips through Google Cloud. AI Weekly described that arrangement as OpenAI's first significant use of chips not made by Nvidia, and said that at the time Google was not renting its most powerful TPUs to OpenAI.

OpenAI is also recruiting a software engineer for TPU compilers in San Francisco. According to AI Weekly, the job listing says the hire will lead the optimization of OpenAI's frontier models on TPUs, covering performance from model code through kernels to hardware execution. OpenAI's hardware division is run by Richard Ho, who previously led development of Google's Cloud TPUs as a senior director of engineering.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the report matters less for the size of any single order, which is unknown, than for what it signals. OpenAI and Google compete directly in chatbots and search, yet OpenAI appears willing to depend on Google for part of its computing. For Nvidia, any shift of OpenAI workloads to other chips would test how firmly its largest customers are tied to its hardware. It is also unclear whether the plan means owning Google hardware outright or expanding a cloud rental, a distinction AI Weekly raised as well.

The timing puts the report close to Alphabet's quarterly results, due on Wednesday, October 28. Reuters said investors want to see whether heavy AI spending is driving growth in Google's cloud business, and Finimize wrote that outside demand for TPUs could shape how the market reads that growth.

The next thing to watch is whether Alphabet or OpenAI confirms the purchase during or after Alphabet's October 28 earnings call, and whether Google offers OpenAI its newest TPUs rather than older capacity.
